This is a job we did back in October. The customer overworked his excavator while digging in clay and cracked the knuckle off, it was only holding by the top plate.

Pic 1

Pic 2

Pic 3

The first step was to secure the thumb and start taking apart the hydraulic hoses. Then we had to remove the pins, which is usually a bundle of joy on a piece of equipment that's misaligned. Take the bolt out and then start bashing away with a 10lbs sledge & a pin driver.

Now that we had it separated, we could set it down on work benches and get a good look at the damage.

Pic 1

Pic 2

Pic 3

After a bit of degreasing it was time to look for cracks with penetrating die. I first did a spot check near the end of the crack and then did the whole knuckle because fuck it, don't want to miss anything.

After leaving the die to penetrate for aboot 10mins, i wiped off the excess and sprayed on the white developer and waited for the cracks to appear as the die was pulled to the surface.

Pic 1

Pic 2

Pic 3

Anywhere you see red seeping out of the white developer is a crack or a pin hole of some sort to gouge out. So next we took it outside set it up on workbenches & covered it up in a cozy fiberglass blanket.

Then it was time for carbon arc gouging , essentially removing the existing welds with an electric arc & compressed air. It's not a clean job but it's ultra fast. Here we can get a glimpse of the hidden damages, the knuckle cover plate is sheared. After it's all gouged out we can take the pieces apart. The knuckle.

We can see the cracks on either side of the plate, more to gouge out and rebuild.

After gouging & grinding it was time to tack the parts back in place & start rebuilding it all.

I started with the interior passes, making sure to get a good root... which is easy to bust through when it's over an 1/8th wide. After a few more passes to fill it up, I grinded away the root on the other sider

Then a few passes to fill the exterior and a bit of finishing on the inside.

After that I rebuilt the boom a bit to fill holes & make the surface nice and smooth.

We crossed our fingers and put the knuckle back on, tacked the butt end in place and clamped the top to see if it would budge by hand. Then we gave it a few good tacks on either side and prepped it for a little trip.

Off to the press !

I used a small piece of tubing to press it down and tack it in place every few inches.

Back onto the workbenches to do the root pass. We went with stick welding because it was deep and didn't want problems with the flux core.

We flipped it on its side to do the flux cored welding much faster than stick and you can lay thick beads. Within an hour both sides were done.

Then the butt end had to be welded up.

We quickly fixed a bore hole to make sure the pins would slide in easily. It was time to hoist it back into place, position it , put in the bottom pin and start reconnecting all the hydraulics.. Once that was done, we could line up the top cylinder a lot more easily.

With the final pin back in place we did a few quick extension tests and called the customer with the final bill... iirc around 2k$.
